web_evidence.title: The Mirror & the Light
web_evidence.note: The publisher’s sustained authorized opening repeatedly presents Cromwell externally as he and he, Cromwell; it also explicitly tags a first-person sentence as his thought, demonstrating the novel’s close third-person technique.

web_evidence.title: The Wolf Hall Trilogy
web_evidence.note: This EU-funded literary-research project describes the trilogy, including The Mirror and the Light, as told entirely through Cromwell’s point of view in a strictly focalized third-person perspective.

web_evidence.title: Review: ‘The Mirror & the Light’ or, the fall of Thomas Cromwell
web_evidence.note: The review explicitly says Cromwell is written in intimate third person and explains that Mantel uses he, Cromwell rather than a first-person I narrator.

web_evidence.title: History Is Written by Hilary Mantel
web_evidence.note: The technical discussion identifies the Cromwell books’ method as third-person free-indirect narration and explains that the trilogy adheres closely to Cromwell’s perspective while referring to him as he.

person_note: The controlling narration is close, present-tense third person, focalized almost entirely through Thomas Cromwell. Numerous sustained quotes externally present Cromwell and other characters as he, she, or by name, agreeing with the authorized opening and the whole-trilogy structural analysis. The isolated story-specific I-passages and several you-passages are free-direct thought, self-address, remembered speech, or focalized generalization; the publisher excerpt itself demonstrates this technique by following a first-person sentence with he thinks. Dialogue and gnomic pronouns likewise do not alter the base person. No researched source indicates sustained first- or second-person chapters, a frame, or alternating narration. The only minor uncertainty is attribution of a few clipped standalone thoughts, but it does not affect the strongly corroborated third-person classification.
